source.title: Stochastic Weight Averaging in Parallel: Large-Batch Training that Generalizes Well
source.authors: Vipul Gupta; Santiago Akle Serrano; D. DeCoste

record.tranche_reason: Compares large- and small-batch training and evaluates whether weight averaging and a small-batch refinement phase recover test accuracy; it uses a different intervention from the cited batch-size studies.
record.gate_note: The paper reports its own test-accuracy comparisons for batch-size recipes. The batch-size claims discussed in Related Work are cited prior results and are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: The study reports its own large- versus small-batch accuracy comparisons and tests recovery through small-batch refinement and weight averaging. CIFAR100 and ImageNet include equal-epoch comparisons relevant to V5.
record.authors_conclusion: The record is substantially accurate. The authors conclude that large-batch initialization does not prevent good generalization: subsequent small-batch refinement and weight averaging can match small-batch-only accuracy on CIFAR10, CIFAR100, and ImageNet while reducing elapsed training time. This uses parallel resources and a tuned transition point; it does not establish equal total computational work.
record.recipe_differences: Uses SGD with large batches, then independent small-batch refinement and weight averaging; compares accuracy across batch-size recipes rather than testing the fixed-epoch penalty alone. The study's contribution is a training algorithm.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcomes vary with dataset, batch and learning-rate schedule, phase transition, and whether small-batch refinement and weight averaging are used.

fits_no_version.finding: Two-dimensional loss-plane visualizations place averaged models nearer the basin center, and gradient-direction cosine similarity decreases late in training.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Weight averaging can reach regions with lower test error within a shared training-loss basin; these visualizations do not measure V7's magnitude-aware sharpness.

fits_no_version.finding: Small-batch SWA improves CIFAR100 accuracy from 76.80% to 79.09%.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Sequential weight averaging improves small-batch training accuracy in this setting.

record.problems: CIFAR10 small- and large-batch-only runs use different epoch budgets. The ImageNet comparison changes batch size, learning rate, and GPU count together. The paper reports averages and ± values but does not identify the uncertainty statistic in the supplied text.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting and its comparison with natural-label held-out accuracy.
Width sweeps beyond the interpolation threshold.
Convolutional versus fully connected architectures and learned local connectivity.

Language models; a batch-size sweep locating a workload-dependent threshold; controlled tests of longer large-batch-only training, warmup, or normalization and regularization changes. CIFAR10 lacks an equal-epoch SGD comparison.
Magnitude-scaled perturbation tolerance, its association with generalization gaps, and ranking against other measures.
Removing examples selected by memorization influence.

missing.what: ImageNet SWAP before-averaging Top5 accuracy is 93.15 ± 0.02, below small-batch SGD's 93.30 ± 0.07. R15 contains it only as a baseline; a separate result would complete the unaveraged hybrid comparisons.

record.verdict_notes: Unequal epoch budgets are an evidential limitation, not a limits_scope result. Failure of large-batch SWA to improve accuracy does not challenge V5, which does not promise that every adaptation succeeds. The reported ± statistic is unspecified; CIFAR results use 10 runs and ImageNet results use three.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label memorization and natural-label generalization coexistence.
Language models, broader workload-dependent batch-size sweeps, and the specific normalization or regularization changes described in the version.
Magnitude-aware sharpness and other generalization measures.
